reasoningSteps: Protocol model and assumptions — Synthetic pipeline: DNS=6 ms, TCP=11 ms, TLS=14 ms, application=27 ms, response transfer=3 ms; no assumed concurrency.

Derivation for the concrete prediction — The sequential trace totals 61 ms, while a response timeout alone cannot establish whether commit occurred; reconcile the order identifier in the application ledger.
Independent cross-check — 6+11+14+27+3=61 ms; removing the 14-ms TLS stage yields 47 ms only in the hypothetical trace, not measured performance.
Disprovable wrong inference — Treating a lost HTTP response as a rolled-back database transaction is false; the transport and persistence boundaries are independent.
Controlled one-variable sensitivity/contrast — Add 4 ms to DNS (10 ms) and predict 65 ms total with the same application result.
Source and validity boundary — RFC 9110 specifies protocol semantics, not the ordering or latency of a particular application stack. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3

software-idempotency.essentialQuestion: If an application offers Idempotency-Key for creating invoices, what may a caller infer after replaying the same key, and what remains unproven?
software-idempotency.verifiedBoundary: An operation is idempotent when repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Retry design matters because networks fail in ambiguous ways: the client may not know whether the server completed the first request.

reasoningSteps: Protocol model and assumptions — Illustrative server contract deduplicates accepted POSTs by the key; requests carry keys [K7,K7]. This is a local contract, not automatic HTTP POST behavior.
Derivation for the concrete prediction — There is one distinct accepted key, so one invoice is created under the stated application contract.
Independent cross-check — Count the distinct nonempty keys, |{K7}|=1; replacing replay with a new key K8 yields two invoices.
Disprovable wrong inference — HTTP POST is not inherently idempotent, and the presence of a header by itself does not prove the server implements replay storage or payload-match checking.
Controlled one-variable sensitivity/contrast — Send [K7,K8] and predict two distinct accepted invoices; verify a reused key with different payload would require a documented conflict rule.

Source and validity boundary — RFC 9110 defines method idempotency; the deduplication model is an illustrative application-specific extension. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2

Independent cross-check — Compare OPTIONS and TRACE, which are also specified as safe methods, noting servers may disable TRACE.

vocabulary.definition: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: application protocol used for transferring requests and responses on the web and in many APIs.
HTTP defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as safe methods because their defined semantics are essentially read-only.
HTTP defines a method as idempotent when multiple identical requests are intended to have the same effect as one such request; PUT, DELETE, and safe methods are idempotent by specification.
The HTTP GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation of the target resource.
HTTP HEAD is identical to GET except the server must not send content in the response.
HTTP POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation according to the resource-specific semantics.

HTTP defines a method as idempotent when multiple identical requests are intended to have the same effect as one such request; PUT, DELETE, and safe methods are idempotent by specification.
The HTTP GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation of the target resource.
HTTP HEAD is identical to GET except the server must not send content in the response.
HTTP POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation according to the resource-specific semantics.
